choices: appear before the committee and explain
patterns.ifNo: Accepting writes the seat vacated, and another election or an appointment fills it.

patterns.title: Your first vote is the big one

roles.fill: the largest question on the record that week: a war, a bailout, an emergency

setting.text: the floor of {the body}, because the vote is cast there.

gates: First weeks in office.
A vote on {the question} on the calendar.

branches.then: The group that helped elect you says you set it back.
A member from elsewhere stands up for you, a tie.
Dozens of others vote with you.

sources.life: Four days after being sworn in as the first woman in Congress in 1917, she voted against entering World War I, speaking briefly as she voted, against House rules. The national suffrage group distanced itself; 49 other members also voted no.

patterns.moment: Days after your oath, {the body} votes on {the question}, and almost everyone is voting one way.
choices: vote no and say why, against the rules
patterns.ifNo: Voting with the majority writes the vote, and your cause's allies say nothing.

patterns.title: The vote that will not end

roles.fill: the member seeking to lead the body
a faction withholding its votes

setting.text: the floor of {the body}, because each round is cast there.

gates: The first day of a new term of {the body}.
The leadership vote has failed at least once.

branches.then: One member can now force a vote to remove the leader, and {holdouts} get seats on the rules committee.
Abstaining helps elect the leader without your name on it.

sources.life: It took 15 ballots over four days in January 2023 to elect him Speaker. No new member could be sworn in until it ended, and the holdouts won rule changes, including letting one member force a vote to remove the Speaker.

patterns.moment: The first act of {the body} is choosing its leader, the vote fails round after round, and no one is sworn in until it ends.
patterns.ifNo: Voting with the leadership writes a loyal vote, and {holdouts} win the rules without you.

patterns.title: Say nothing until you have something to say

roles.fill: the leader who picked you, or the chamber's senior figure

setting.text: Where {senior member} would take you aside.

gates: First term in a legislature.

branches.then: A member says the way to get along is to go along, and asks whether you will.
From high above the floor you learn who is who, a record of ties.

sources.life: Picked by Tammany leader Tom Foley for the New York Assembly, the young Smith got one piece of advice: do not speak until you have something to say. He sat as a back-bencher learning who was who.
The advice to get along by going along is tied to him, though no record of him saying it to new members is known.

patterns.moment: {senior member} tells you on your first day not to speak on the floor until you have something to say.
choices: follow it and learn the room
speak on your first bill anyway
ask what they want from you
patterns.ifNo: Following it writes a quiet first season, and colleagues learn your name slowly.

patterns.title: The chair who did not want you

roles.fill: the chair of the committee, said with years in the gavel
another member the chair opposed

setting.text: the committee's first meeting, because the slight is made in front of the members.

gates: You were put on a committee over its chair's objection.
{other newcomer} is on the same committee.

branches.when: the slight is one chair for two
branches.then: You and {other newcomer} share a single chair at the table, and the room sees it.

branches.when: {other newcomer} got the seat only because the leader stepped in
branches.then: You two are allies from here.
Reforms take the gavel away, and your silent protest is remembered.

sources.life: In 1973 Armed Services chairman F. Edward Hébert set out a single chair for the two newcomers he had opposed. They shared it as a silent protest, and Hébert lost his chairmanship in 1975.

patterns.moment: {committee chair}, who did not want you on the committee, slights you and {other newcomer} in front of everyone at the first meeting.
choices: take it together as a silent protest
patterns.ifNo: Standing by the wall writes nothing filed, and the chair has won the morning.

patterns.title: The first meeting is organized without you

roles.fill: the leader of the majority bloc against you

setting.text: {the body}'s first meeting, because the organizing vote is there.

gates: You are the new executive.
A majority of {the body} opposed you.

branches.then: The bloc names the chairs, and years of deadlock follow.

branches.when: a court or a special election changes the numbers
branches.then: The deadlock breaks.

sources.life: At his first Chicago council meeting in 1983, he and 21 allied aldermen walked out; the other 29 named the committee chairs, and the bloc blocked his appointments until special elections in 1986.

patterns.moment: At {the body}'s first meeting, {bloc leader}'s majority names the committee chairs without you.
choices: govern by veto and wait for the next election
patterns.ifNo: Staying silent writes that the bloc organized {the body} unopposed.

patterns.title: The hole in the budget

roles.fill: the official who runs the place's budget

setting.text: Wherever the executive works in the first week.

gates: An executive office in your first weeks.
A deficit on the budget record.

branches.then: The tax you said you would not raise is the only way left.
The people laid off are names in your place.
You push them out of the jobs they hold.

sources.life: Sworn in as California governor just after midnight in 1967, he found a shortfall, froze hiring and ordered cuts, then signed what was called the largest tax increase proposed by any governor.
Facing an inherited deficit in 1975, she laid off state workers and returned her own raise.
He inherited a deficit in 1934 and cut more than 1,000 positions in his first year.

patterns.moment: In your first week, {budget director} shows you the deficit you inherited.
choices: freeze hiring and cut every department
cut your own perks and pay first
patterns.ifNo: Putting it off writes nothing yet, and the hole grows on the record.

patterns.title: The promise on day one

roles.fill: the main pledge of your campaign on record

setting.text: Where the executive signs orders, on the first day.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{the promise} is on record.

branches.then: You sign the order minutes after the oath. The cost lands on the budget and on the places that relied on the money.

branches.when: the police unit you ran against
branches.then: You disband it in your first weeks.
You veto budgets until the tax you promised against passes. Tens of thousands rally against you, and you may not run again.

sources.life: Minutes after his swearing-in as California governor in 2003, he signed an order repealing the tripled vehicle license fee, his main pledge.
After taking office as Detroit's mayor in 1974, he disbanded the police decoy unit he had campaigned against.

Elected in 1990 after saying he would not seek an income tax, he faced a large deficit, vetoed budgets without one, and signed a 6 percent income tax in 1991. Tens of thousands rallied against him, and he did not run again.

patterns.moment: {the promise} can be kept at once, by order, minutes after the oath, or broken when the numbers turn.
choices: keep it at once by order
patterns.ifNo: Delaying writes the promise as still open, and the people who voted for it count the days.

patterns.title: The order on the first day

roles.fill: a say members hold by custom over permits, licenses or jobs in their own districts

setting.text: Where the executive signs orders, on the first day.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{the power} is on record.

branches.when: members are surprised at its reach
branches.then: They line up against your first bill.
Reformers say it is half done; members say you went too far.

sources.life: Right after her 2019 inauguration as Chicago mayor, she signed an order curbing aldermen's long-held say over permits and licenses in their wards, leaving zoning alone. Many aldermen were surprised at its reach.

patterns.moment: You can sign an order on your first day that takes a long-held power away from the members of {the body}.
patterns.ifNo: Leaving it alone writes that the custom stands, and the reformers who backed you ask why.

patterns.title: The perks you refuse

roles.fill: the office you now hold
your chief of staff

setting.text: Where the executive works in the first week.

gates: You hold an office with perks on record.

branches.when: a hole in the office rug
branches.then: You leave it, and members who come asking for favors see it.

branches.when: you live on part of your pay
branches.then: You give the rest away, a public pledge on your record.

sources.life: As California's new governor in 1975, he refused the new governor's residence, rented an apartment, and drove a Plymouth instead of riding in a limousine.
She returned a $7,000 raise and sold the state's limousine and plane.
After winning her council seat she said she would live on about $40,000 of her salary.

patterns.moment: The residence, the car and the raise come with {the office}, and {chief of staff} asks which you will take.
patterns.ifNo: Taking it all writes nothing, and the press may count it.

patterns.title: Who gets the work

roles.fill: a large public project on record
firms owned by people the old contracts shut out

setting.text: Wherever the executive meets the builders.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{the project} is on record with contracts {the left out} had no part in.

branches.when: business and state leaders push back
branches.then: Lawsuits threaten, and the work sits idle.

branches.when: the work resumes with a share
branches.then: Years later, the share of work those firms did is the record.

sources.life: In 1975 Atlanta's mayor halted work and withheld payment on the airport expansion to bring minority firms into its contracts. Despite pushback from business and state leaders, work resumed with a required minority share, and by 1980 minority firms did about a quarter of the work.

patterns.moment: {the project} was contracted before you took office, and almost none of the work goes to {the left out}.
choices: stop the work until the contracts are redone
set a share for new contracts only
let it go ahead and fight later
patterns.ifNo: Letting it go ahead writes the contracts as they were, and the people who elected you count it.

patterns.title: The strike on day one

roles.fill: a public workers' union on record
its leader, said with years at its head

setting.text: Wherever the talks are held.

gates: You take office.
A public contract on record that runs out that day, or a strike on the record.

branches.then: A judge orders {the union}'s leaders arrested, and the strike hardens.
Wages rise, and the state passes a law limiting public strikes.
The press says you talked down to them instead of bargaining.

sources.life: New York's transit workers struck on his first day as mayor in 1966. Their leader, Mike Quill, was jailed; after twelve days the union took a mediators' package, and the state later passed a law restricting public-employee strikes.

patterns.moment: The contract with {the union} runs out the day you take office, and the workers walk out.
choices: ask a judge to enforce the law
patterns.ifNo: Waiting writes nothing, and the place stops running.

patterns.title: The storm that decides the next race

roles.fill: whoever means to run against you
a storm, flood, fire, heat wave or outage on the world's record

setting.text: Wherever the response is run from, or out with the crews.

gates: You hold the executive office.
{the disaster} is on the record in your place.

branches.then: The plows fall behind, trains stop on some lines, and the snow sits for weeks.
The response is your campaign.
Those voters remember it at the primary.

sources.life: A January 1979 blizzard paralyzed Chicago and the plows fell behind. Byrne used the anger to beat the sitting mayor, Bilandic, in the primary weeks later.

patterns.moment: The first disaster of your term, {the disaster}, hits {the place}, the response falls behind, and {challenger} is watching.
choices: say the place is handling it
open the books on the response
patterns.ifNo: Saying it is handled writes your words against the record of the streets.

patterns.title: Your own party overrides you

roles.fill: a bill or budget line on record that you vetoed
the leader of the body's majority, of your own party, said with the post

setting.text: Wherever the news reaches you the day of the override: your office, a car between events.

gates: You hold an executive office with a veto.
You vetoed {the bill}, and {the body} voted to override it.
Your party holds the majority in {the body}.
weights: How many of your vetoes the body has overridden.
How far your views sit from the majority's.
Traits that hate waste or dig in.

branches.then: The picture runs everywhere. Voters like it, and the senior members whose projects you mocked remember it at the next vote.
The body overrides you the next day in a special sitting, and the press calls it a failed protest.
The override is your first break with the majority, and members learn that your veto can be beaten.
You veto lines in members' own districts, and those members stop returning your calls.

sources.life: As South Carolina governor, his own party's House overrode 105 of his 106 budget vetoes in one day in 2004. The next day he brought live pigs into the chamber to protest pork spending. In 2006 he rejected the whole budget, and the legislature overrode him the next day.
In 2013, his first year as Indiana governor, the Republican legislature overrode his veto of a local tax bill by wide margins in both houses.

patterns.moment: {the body}, where your own party holds the majority, overrides your veto of {the bill}, and {chamber leader} tells the press the votes were never in doubt.
choices: veto the next one too and take it to the public with a stunt
name the members who voted to override, in their own districts
meet {chamber leader} and trade: you sign one of theirs, they hold one of yours
stop vetoing and work on bills before they pass
patterns.ifNo: Letting it go writes that your vetoes do not hold. The next budget comes with more in it, and members stop asking what you think first.

patterns.title: The law you signed, and the backlash

roles.fill: a law you signed, on record
a big employer, convention or league on the place's record, said with what it does there

setting.text: Where the pressure finds you: a television interview, a call from {employer}, a meeting with your backers.

gates: You hold an executive office.
You signed {the law}.
An employer or group on record has said it will pull out, cancel or protest over it.
weights: How many jobs {employer} holds in the place.
How close your next race is.
How strongly your backers wanted the law.

branches.when: you say on the air you will not change it, then sign a fix
branches.then: Both sides quote your first words against you.
The lost jobs are on the record, and the members who passed the law blame you for the fix or for the signing.

branches.when: you disagreed with part of it
branches.then: You sign it anyway, saying a veto was not yours to cast, and your own side splits over it.

branches.when: a health emergency asks you to bend your views
branches.then: An outbreak spreads where clinics closed. Allow, for a time, the measure you opposed, or hold to your view.

sources.life: In 2015 he signed an Indiana religious-objections law that businesses and conventions called anti-gay. He said on television the law would not change, then signed a revision days later; a company canceled a planned expansion, and backers of the original were angry. The same year he let counties open needle exchanges during an HIV outbreak, which he had opposed.

In 2006 the Louisiana governor signed a ban on most abortions to take effect if the Supreme Court allowed it. She thought exceptions for rape and incest were reasonable but felt she should not veto it.

patterns.moment: Days after you sign {the law}, {employer} says it will take its jobs or its event elsewhere, and your own backers say any change is a betrayal.
choices: sign a fix that narrows it
say nothing and wait for it to pass
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you stood by it. {employer} acts on its threat, and the lost jobs go on the record with your name.

patterns.title: The deciding vote

roles.fill: a bill or nomination set for a vote on record
the leader who needs the vote, said with the post

setting.text: Where the leader catches you before the roll: the floor, the leader's office, a call that night.

gates: You hold a seat in {the body}, or preside over it with a vote to break ties.
{the bill} is set for a vote.
The count is one short or tied without you.
weights: How your district feels about the bill.

branches.when: you hold out for a change
branches.then: The change goes in, a part of the bill is struck, and the bill's backers blame you for what it lost.
The money for your place is in the bill, your party's base calls it a sellout, and a challenger from your own side starts to talk to donors.

branches.when: you preside and the vote ties
branches.then: You break the tie, the first time one was needed for that kind of vote, and both sides note it.

branches.when: you voted no the first time and it failed
branches.then: On the second vote you switch to yes, and the record shows both.

sources.life: In 2009 he was the 60th vote needed to end debate on the health care bill, and his opposition to a government-run insurance option got it dropped from the law.

In 2009 he was one of three Republicans to vote for the stimulus, winning about $10 billion for medical research. Most Pennsylvania Republicans disapproved, and a primary challenger announced weeks later.
In 2017, presiding over a tied Senate, he cast the first tie-breaking vote ever needed to confirm a cabinet member.
In 2008 she voted against the bank rescue the first time the House took it up, then voted yes on the second vote.

patterns.moment: {chamber leader} is one vote short on {the bill}, or the count is tied, and yours is the vote left.
choices: hold out for a change in the bill
trade your vote for money for your place
patterns.ifNo: Staying away writes an absence on the record, and the bill passes or fails without you. Both sides remember where you were.

patterns.title: One seat decides who runs the body

roles.fill: a member whose party or caucus could change, said with the seat and years served
whoever presides over {the body} and breaks ties, said with the post

setting.text: Where a member would be worked in private: an office after hours, a dinner, a long phone call.

gates: You hold a seat in {the body} or lead a party in it.
The seats are split so that one member changes who holds the majority.
weights: How far {wavering member}'s views sit from their party's.

branches.then: Your party runs the body, and the chairs change hands in the middle of the session.
Control turns on who holds that post, so your side leads for days and loses it when the term changes.

branches.when: the one who moved asks to keep their seniority
branches.then: Your own members refuse to give up their chairs, and the newcomer starts at the bottom.

branches.when: control flips and you gain a chair
branches.then: You chair a committee you did not expect, and its first big bill is yours to carry.

sources.life: With the Senate split 50-50 in January 2001, the outgoing vice president's tie-breaking vote made him majority leader for 17 days. In June a Vermont Republican left his caucus to become an independent, and control came back to Daschle.
When control flipped in June 2001 he became chair of the government affairs committee and pushed to fold border, emergency and coast agencies into one new department.
After he switched parties in 2009, his new colleagues refused to let him keep nearly 30 years of committee seniority.

patterns.moment: {the body} is split down the middle, and {wavering member} is weighing a move that would hand control to the other side.
choices: promise help in their next race
ask your own wavering members what they need first
patterns.ifNo: Making no offer writes that you let it ride. If {wavering member} moves, you learn of it from the news.

patterns.title: A move in the rules

roles.fill: a bill or deadline on record that your side cannot pass or stop the ordinary way
a rule change, a split bill, a held vote or a skipped step that the body's rules allow

setting.text: The room where the body's rules are set: a rules committee, a joint committee, the leader's office the night before.

gates: You lead your party in {the body} or hold the executive office.
{the fight} is on the calendar.
The rules allow {the move}.
weights: What the fight costs residents each day.
How the public blames each side.

branches.when: you hold the vote that would end it
branches.then: The rules make you the only one who can bring the other side's bill up. You keep it down, the government shuts, and critics say you made it longer.

branches.when: the other side has left to block the vote
branches.then: You strip the spending parts so the vote no longer needs them in the room, and it passes in minutes.

branches.when: a court says the move broke the rules
branches.then: A judge voids the law over how it passed, and a higher court puts it back.

sources.life: The night before the 2013 shutdown, a House rules change made the majority leader the only member who could force a vote on the Senate's funding bill. He did not allow it, which critics said made the shutdown longer.

When Wisconsin Senate Democrats left the state in 2011 to deny a quorum, Republicans stripped the spending provisions so the bill could pass without one. A judge struck the law down over open-meetings rules, and the state supreme court reinstated it.

patterns.moment: Your side can only win {the fight} by a move in the rules: {the move}.
choices: pass the fight to the other side and let the deadline hit
split the bill and pass the part you can
patterns.ifNo: Dropping it writes that your side gave way. The other side says so at every stop.

patterns.title: When the empty seat's vote is held

roles.fill: a seat on record that is vacant or that you are leaving
a popular figure of the other party who would be on that ballot, said with the office

setting.text: Wherever the law makes you decide: your office, with the clerk's calendar in front of you.

gates: A seat is vacant or you have said you will leave one.
You hold the power to set the date, to appoint, or to time your own leaving.
weights: What a separate election costs the place.
How the date changes who turns out.
Seniority at stake for the one who follows.

branches.then: It costs the place millions, and the press says you did it to keep {popular rival} off the ballot on your own election day.

branches.when: the one leaving resigns a day early
branches.then: You, as the appointee, are sworn in a day before the new class and outrank them for years.

branches.when: you ask for the vote on the general election day
branches.then: The winner takes the seat at once, ahead of the rest of the new class.

sources.life: In 2013 the New Jersey governor ordered a $25 million special election for a vacant U.S. Senate seat, 20 days before his own race, a move widely seen as keeping a popular Democrat off his ballot day.
In 1985 the outgoing senator resigned a day early, and Governor Dukakis appointed Kerry to the seat, giving him seniority over the other new senators.
After losing his 2014 primary he resigned early and asked the governor to hold the special election on the general election day.

patterns.moment: {the seat} is empty, or soon will be, and when its vote is held, or the day you leave, is yours to set.
choices: hold the vote with the regular election
resign early so the one who follows starts sooner
appoint someone to hold the seat
patterns.ifNo: Leaving it to the law's default writes nothing new. The seat waits, and the place goes without a voice until then.

patterns.title: Taking on the public workers

roles.fill: the unions of the place's public workers, said with who they represent
a member of your own party who will not vote for it, said with the seat

setting.text: The building where the body meets, full of people, or your office with the noise outside.

gates: You hold an executive office.
A budget gap is on record.
The place's public workers bargain through unions.
weights: How many public workers the place has.
Your party's share of the body.

branches.when: the other party's members leave the place to block the vote
branches.then: Without them the body cannot take up spending, and the standoff runs for weeks (C05).
Your first defection. The bill passes anyway, or fails by one.

branches.when: you once promised these workers no change
branches.then: Their union sues and quotes your promise (C38).
A recall drive starts against you and the members who voted for it (C31).

branches.when: you make a deal with the other party's leaders
branches.then: They raise what workers pay and end bargaining over health plans, and their own base turns on them.

sources.life: In 2011 the Wisconsin governor proposed sharp limits on public unions' bargaining, leaving out police and firefighters. Protesters filled the Capitol, all 14 Democratic senators went to Illinois to deny a quorum, and one Republican voted no. A recall followed.

In 2010 the New Jersey governor signed pension changes after promising police and firefighters none, and their unions sued. In 2011 he made a deal with Democratic leaders raising what workers paid and ending bargaining over health benefits.

patterns.moment: You send {the body} a bill that cuts what public workers can bargain for, and {union} fills the building.
choices: take the unions' money offer and drop the bargaining limits
make a deal with the other party's leaders
patterns.ifNo: Dropping it writes that you backed down. The gap is still in the next budget.

patterns.title: Money from above, with strings

roles.fill: the government above yours, said by its leader's post
a rail line, a relief program or a health program on the offer's record

setting.text: Wherever you announce it: a press conference, a letter to {higher government}.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{higher government} has offered the money on record.
weights: How many jobs it would pay for.
How strongly your backers oppose it.

branches.then: The money goes to other places, and repairs it would have covered come out of your own budget.

branches.when: the body sues to take it
branches.then: The highest court in the place rules that only the body can turn the money down.

branches.when: you take it on your own terms
branches.then: You strike a version with {higher government}, and both sides call it a win.

sources.life: Elected Wisconsin governor in 2010, he said he would refuse an $810 million federal rail grant. The money went to other states, and the state paid at least $60 million for rail repairs.
In 2009 he became the first governor to formally reject part of his state's federal stimulus money. South Carolina's supreme court ruled that only the legislature could decline it.

patterns.moment: {higher government} offers {the place} money for {the program}, and taking it means rules and costs you campaigned against.
patterns.ifNo: Not deciding writes that you took it by default, and your backers say so.

patterns.title: Running for a leadership post

roles.fill: a party post in {the body}: leader, whip, caucus chair
the member expected to win, said with the post they hold now

setting.text: Where members are counted: the members' dining room, the cloakroom, calls through the night.

gates: You hold a seat in {the body}.
{the post} is open or contested.
weights: Money you raised for members' races.

branches.then: You lose by a wide margin. The next time a lower post opens, you take it without a fight.

branches.when: the leader appoints you as a deputy
branches.then: You count votes for years and learn who owes whom.

branches.when: you raised money for members' races
branches.then: The members you helped back you for the next post up.
You are third in line in the party's leadership, and every break you make with {party leader} is now news (C15).

sources.life: He ran for House minority leader in 2006 and lost 168 to 27. In 2009 he won the third-ranking post without opposition.
The whip appointed him chief deputy whip in 2002. He was elected whip in 2008 and became majority leader in 2011, after raising more than $30 million for the party's House campaigns.
Two years into her first term, in 2018, House Republicans elected her conference chair, the third-ranking post.

patterns.moment: {the post} is open, and {favorite} has most of the votes counted already.
choices: run against the favorite on a cause
back the favorite and ask for a lower post
help other members win their races first
patterns.ifNo: Not running writes nothing against you. The winner remembers who stood where.

patterns.title: Meeting the government yours shuns

roles.fill: the head of a government or rival power on record in conflict with yours
a member of the other party who attacks the trip, said with the seat

setting.text: {adversary leader}'s own capital, because going there is the act.

gates: You hold an office.
{adversary leader} heads a government on record in conflict with yours.
weights: What trade or relief is at stake.
How hostile your party is to the other side.

branches.then: The executive calls it propaganda, and the vote you hoped to move goes the other way.
They say you broke the rule against private dealings with foreign governments, and it follows you.

branches.when: years later you go as the executive's envoy
branches.then: It is the first such meeting in decades, and a leak about what you said starts calls for an inquiry.

sources.life: In 2004 the Louisiana governor went to Cuba to build trade and met Fidel Castro, a controversial trip at home.

As a new senator in 1985 he went to Nicaragua with Tom Harkin and met Daniel Ortega, and the trip was criticized. In 2013, as secretary of state, he met Iran's foreign minister, the first such meeting since 1979.
In 2007 he suggested that Nancy Pelosi's meeting with Syria's president might break the law against private diplomacy.

patterns.moment: You could go and meet {adversary leader}, whom your own government shuns, to open trade or to carry a message home.
patterns.ifNo: Declining writes nothing. The opening goes to someone else.

patterns.title: Family on the inside

roles.fill: a child, sibling or partner who works in your campaign, your business or your government, said with the job
someone offering a meeting, a post or a favor, said with who they work for

setting.text: Where family business happens: the family's office, a dinner, a phone call you hear about later.

gates: You hold an office or are running.
{family member} holds a role in your campaign, business or government on record.
weights: How much the family business touches your office.

branches.when: the meeting promised dirt on your rival
branches.then: Emails show what it was for, and years later a committee refers {family member} to prosecutors.

branches.when: a post is said to be made for them
branches.then: Critics say the job was created for them while you held office, and it follows them into their own race.

branches.when: {family member} runs for your old seat
branches.then: They win the seat you once held, and every vote they cast is read against yours (C47).

sources.life: During the 2016 race his eldest son, who also ran the family company, took a meeting offered with the promise of damaging material on the rival. Emails released in 2017 showed its purpose.
In 2002, while her father was vice president, she took a State Department post that critics said was created for her. In 2016 she won the Wyoming House seat he had held from 1979 to 1989.

patterns.moment: {family member} works for your campaign or near your office, and {go-between} offers them something you would never take yourself.
choices: set a rule that family stays out of the work
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you let them decide. What they do goes on your record as well as theirs.

patterns.title: The one investigating you answers to you

roles.fill: the head of an investigating office you can appoint and remove, said with the office
an investigation on record
someone you could name in their place, said with the seat they hold

setting.text: Your office, with {investigator} or about them.

gates: You hold an executive office that appoints {investigator}.
{the matter} names your campaign, your staff or your acts.
weights: How close it gets to you.

branches.then: A second, wider investigation opens because of the firing, run by someone you cannot remove.
{replacement} is interviewed, called the top pick, and withdraws within the week.

branches.when: you are the one offered the post
branches.then: Taking it means leaving your seat or your firm, and the one offering is a client of your firm.

sources.life: In May 2017 he fired FBI director James Comey and then said he was concerned about Comey's role in the Russia investigations. The firing led to a special counsel.
Days after the firing, the former senator was interviewed to replace Comey and called the top pick. His law firm had Trump as a client, and he withdrew a week later.

patterns.moment: {investigator}, who answers to you, is looking into {the matter}, and it touches your campaign or your people.
choices: hand the case to someone outside your reach
ask them in private to ease off
patterns.ifNo: Leaving them alone writes nothing new. The investigation goes where the evidence goes.

patterns.title: The inquiry you could open

roles.fill: whoever holds the office whose conduct is in question, said with the post
the leader of the other party in the body, said with the post

setting.text: Where you would be asked: a private meeting, a call, the hallway outside a closed hearing.

gates: You hold a seat with power to investigate: a chair, a party leader, a member named to a panel.
Conduct by {powerful officeholder} is on record.
weights: The mood in the place after a crisis.

branches.when: they ask you not to look, citing a war or crisis
branches.then: You agree to a narrower review by one committee, and later say you were asked.

branches.when: {other-party leader} names you to their panel
branches.then: You become its vice chair, and your own party calls it betrayal (C15).

branches.when: the trail leads to your own party's people
branches.then: You follow it anyway, and your party's elders criticize you.

branches.when: you hold hearings without sworn testimony
branches.then: Both sides say you went soft, and you mention removal as a remedy on the air.

sources.life: He said the vice president asked him not to investigate the September 11 attacks; the Intelligence Committee did a limited review instead.
In 2021 Speaker Nancy Pelosi named her to the House committee on the January 6 attack, and she became its vice chair.
His staff followed money to a bank, BCCI, that was shut in 1991. The 1992 report also named influential Democrats, and some in his party criticized him for it.
In 2006, as Judiciary chair, he called warrantless wiretapping inappropriate and held hearings without forcing sworn testimony from the attorney general, while mentioning impeachment as a remedy.

patterns.moment: You can open an inquiry into what {powerful officeholder} did, and {powerful officeholder} asks you not to.
choices: hold hearings but do not compel sworn testimony
patterns.ifNo: Dropping it writes that you let it go. If the facts come out later, the record shows you were asked and said yes.

patterns.title: Your own party's leader on trial

roles.fill: the executive from your party, said with the office

setting.text: the floor of {the body} on the day of the vote, because the vote is public.

gates: You hold a seat in a body that can impeach or try an executive.
{party leader} is charged in that body.
weights: How loyal your district is to {party leader}.

branches.then: Members of your party demand your post, your party at home censures you, and a challenger is recruited (C15, C29).

branches.when: you speak against them but vote to keep them
branches.then: The speech is quoted against you years later, in a primary from the other side of your party.

branches.when: you cast a vote of your own kind
branches.then: The record writes it as a no, and both sides call you slippery.

sources.life: In January 2021 she voted to impeach President Trump after the Capitol attack. Colleagues demanded her removal from leadership, and Wyoming's party censured her.
In 1998 he was the first prominent Democrat to criticize President Clinton in a Senate speech, then voted against removal. The speech was used against him in his 2006 primary.
At President Clinton's 1999 trial he cited Scottish law to vote not proven. The Senate recorded it as not guilty.

patterns.moment: {the body} is voting on whether to impeach or remove {party leader}, the head of your own party.
choices: speak against what they did but vote against removal
cast a vote of your own kind
patterns.ifNo: Not voting writes an absence in the most watched vote of your term.

patterns.title: Your caucus votes on you

roles.fill: a party post or committee chair you hold in {the body}
the leader of your party you broke with, said with the post
a member of your party who wants your post, said with the seat

setting.text: the closed meeting of your party's members, because the vote happens there.

gates: You hold a party post or a chair in {the body}.
You broke with {party leader} on a recorded vote, endorsement or statement.
weights: How many members agree with you.
How popular {party leader} is with the party's voters.

branches.then: You keep the post by a wide margin. Days later your party at home censures you anyway.
No count is kept. You are out, and {loyal member} takes the post.

branches.when: a powerful officeholder asks them to spare you
branches.then: You keep your chair but lose a seat on another committee.
Your new colleagues refuse to give you your old seniority (C04).

sources.life: In February 2021 she kept her leadership post 145 to 61 in a secret ballot, and days later Wyoming's party censured her. In May she was removed by voice vote and replaced.
After he backed the Republican nominee in 2008, Senate Democrats voted 42 to 13 to let him keep his chairmanship, after President-elect Obama urged them not to punish him. He lost one committee seat.
When he joined the Democrats in 2009, they refused to let him keep his seniority on committees.

patterns.moment: Members of your own party in {the body} call a vote on whether you keep {your post}, after you broke with {party leader}.
choices: make your case in a speech
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you let them decide, and the vote goes by who is loudest.

patterns.title: The boss is away

roles.fill: the officeholder you work for, said with the office
whoever stands next in line to act for {the executive}, said with the post

setting.text: The executive's office, with the executive's chair empty.

gates: You are the chief of staff, the deputy or {second in line} to {the executive}.
{the executive} is away on record: campaigning, traveling, unreachable.

branches.when: {the executive} is running for higher office
branches.then: You run the place day to day for months. Later you say so, and it is the record you run on.
After many unanswered calls you have to tell the press something. Whatever you say is quoted when the truth comes out (C22).
They ask whether the office is vacant in law, and the question itself is news.

sources.life: As chief of staff to California's governor, he later said he ran the state while his boss campaigned for president in 1980.
In 2009 the South Carolina governor told his staff he was hiking and did not answer 15 calls from his chief of staff while he was in Argentina.

patterns.moment: {the executive} is away, and the calls, the decisions and the press all come to you.
choices: decide what must be decided and say so
tell the press the truth about where they are
patterns.ifNo: Holding everything writes that the work waited. What waited is on the record.

patterns.title: The disaster bigger than your government

roles.fill: the government above yours, said by its leader's post
a storm, flood, fire, outage or shortage on the world's record

setting.text: Wherever the response is run from, or out where the damage is.

gates: You hold an executive office.

patterns.title: The first word on the address

roles.fill: whoever is around the player with a stand on the address: kin or a housemate at home; a neighbor; a coworker the next morning; a regular where people gather (the barber, the diner counter, a morning coffee group, a church's fellowship hour); a local party officer; rarely a stranger, and only where talking to strangers is normal in that setting. the President's address on record that day: the inaugural on day 0, later any big address
one point of {the address} from its record: what the President promised, warned about or claimed, and which side the President took

The setting's habits: home and regulars' places more, work and strangers less.

start calling people for work that day
patterns.ifNo: Telling no one writes silence on the tie record, and {the first to hear} learns it from someone else and remembers.

patterns.title: Someone dying, someone buried

roles.fill: whoever on the health or death record is gravely ill or has just died: a parent, a grandparent, a partner, a sibling, a friend. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
whoever on the household record carries the daily care: the player, a relative, or a housemate
whoever else the records tie to {the dying or dead}: kin, an old friend, a neighbor, a church or lodge member, a coworker
whoever the records show could ease it: a hospice program, neighbors, a faith group, a friend's family, or none

setting.text: Wherever {the dying or dead} is on the records: the home, a care bed, the place of burial and the gathering after. The talk with {the mourner} happens wherever they meet the player, a doorway, a kitchen, the steps after the service.

gates: The health or death record shows {the dying or dead} gravely ill or dead.
{the dying or dead} is tied to the player or the player's household on the records.
The player can reach the place on the travel record within the days it matters.
A date for the care or the service is on the calendar.
weights: How long the illness has run.
Whether the player lives in the same home as {the dying or dead}.
Whether {the helper} has a record of showing up.
Whether the player holds an office and the dead had a cause.

branches.then: The days of care write on the player's time and money records and on the household's tie to {the dying or dead}.
The absence is on the tie record and a grief later names it, and a no-show at a service is remembered by {the mourner}.

branches.when: {the helper} is neighbors or a faith group
branches.then: The household's later debts of thanks go on the favor record.

branches.when: {the dying or dead} left a cause
branches.then: A mourner asks the player to carry it, which unlocks an invitation scene.

branches.when: the player has just won a seat
branches.then: The death can reach the player between the win and the oath, and the chamber leader's call about the seat reads it.

sources.life: As a boy Grant lost his mother to cancer, did not go to her funeral and regrets it. His father later gave him a note she had written. His friend's mother became like a second mother to him, and her death years later moved him deeply.

About twenty years earlier she moved her ailing father into the family home and the household cared for him for seven years until he died. She says she did not think she had another choice and felt isolated while friends praised her. Her son valued the dignity of the death at home.

A daughter recorded a talk with her father in hospice at his New Jersey home, days before he died. Asked what he was proudest of, he said his children and family. He had paid off the home and died there with loved ones around him.

In 2007 his brother, with terminal cancer and in home hospice, moved from California to Utah near his adult children. Neighborhood women cleaned and furnished a small house before the family arrived at night. The brother died two days later with family around him.

patterns.moment: {the dying or dead} is dying or gone, and the player must say who is there, who stays, and who speaks.
choices: go for the service and speak to {the mourner}
ask what is needed before deciding
patterns.ifNo: Not going is written on the tie record. A mourner names it later, and a grief the player did not attend does not close.

patterns.title: Under one roof, or not

roles.fill: whoever on the tie record is the player's partner or would-be partner. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
whoever else lives where the player or {the partner} lives: parents, children from before, a housemate, a grandparent

roles.slot: the one who objects or backs
roles.fill: a relative or friend the records show has a stand on the match: a parent, a sibling, an old friend
a child of the player or {the partner}, if the records show one; otherwise none

setting.text: Wherever {the partner} and the player are when it comes up, by the records: at home, in public, at a venue, or the doorway of a household that will have to make room. The ending of it happens at home, with whoever lives there.

gates: {the partner} is tied to the player on the tie record as a partner or a would-be partner.
The housing record shows either a home or a room that could hold both, or a household that must change.
{the partner} has made the ask, or the break, on the calendar.
The player has not answered it before.
weights: How long the tie has run.
Whether {the child} is in either household.
Whether either household's money is tight.
Whether {the one who objects or backs} lives in the same home.
Traits that commit or hold back.

branches.then: The household record changes: one joins the other, or a new home is found, and the money record is shared from that date.
A date to revisit goes on the calendar and the tie record shows a doubt.
The tie record cools, and the one who asked remembers it at the next big choice.
The household record splits, the child's days are set between homes, and who keeps the home goes on the housing record.

branches.when: {the one who objects or backs} is in the house
branches.then: They speak up, and their stand reaches the family's later votes of confidence.

sources.life: A restaurant owner and a woman he met at an engagement party in 1971 married about a week later. He moved in with her, her mother and her grandfather until they could afford their own home. Her mother opposed it at first and later came to love him, and they were still together near their fiftieth anniversary.
After three months together he proposed during a recorded interview, using the ring his late father had used. She said yes. They married, stayed together nearly twenty years and have two sons.

A mother who divorced through a mediator tells another who is divorcing how she and her ex told their daughter together, sitting on the floor and stressing routines that stay the same. They share custody on a written plan and stayed on civil terms.

Her son, twelve, recalls the yelling at home before his parents' 2009 divorce, being torn, and his grades slipping for two school years. He now spends alternate weeks with each parent and mostly wants his mother to be happy.

patterns.moment: {the partner} asks to share a roof, to marry, or to end it, and the household has to rearrange around the answer.
choices: say yes and name what changes in the home
say yes when a stated thing is settled
say not yet and give a time
patterns.ifNo: A no or a put-off is written on the tie record and read at the next big choice by both of them.

patterns.title: The one you fell out with

roles.fill: whoever the tie record shows as cut off, hurt or in conflict with the player or someone the player loves: a sibling, a cousin, a former friend, a neighbor. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
whoever the records show stands between: a grandparent, a parent who took a side, a child, a friend of both, or none
what the records show split them: a harsh act, an unkept promise, a difference of belief, a money matter, a move
whoever is present or hears of it: kin at a meal, neighbors, a coworker

setting.text: Wherever {the estranged} and the player can meet or talk, by the records: a doorway, a phone call, a gathering where both are expected, a public place with others looking on.

gates: The tie record shows {the estranged} and the player (or someone the player loves) at odds.
{the cause} is on the record.
A way to reach {the estranged} exists: an address, a number, or a go-between.
The player has not already settled it with {the estranged}.
weights: How long they have been apart.
Whether the player's work or office adds to the pressure.
Traits that forgive or hold on.

branches.then: The tie record warms or stays cold depending on the reply, and a later scene reads who moved first.
The grudge record softens and an old ally may return later.

branches.when: {the go-between} is a child or a grandparent
branches.then: The player is asked to put the quarrel aside for them, and the answer is written.

branches.when: {the estranged} was cast out for who they are
branches.then: The player's stand, for or against, is on the tie record and read by others in the family.
{the estranged} may be asked to endorse or oppose, and the quarrel enters the race.

sources.life: The oldest of eight was put out of his father's house as a teen after being found out. As each younger sibling left or was thrown out, he reached out to be their big brother again. Some resisted at first, but the eight became close.

Two brothers who grew up in a hard home. After their mother died of cancer the older one tormented the younger. Their grandmother urged the younger to call before the older deployed. Each admitted jealousy of the other, and they became close.

A high school senior stuck between her mother and her aunt, who had fallen out. Her mother saw her contact with the aunt as disloyalty. The aunt said she would never shut her niece out over the quarrel and told her to make her own choices.

A Brooklyn father set days when his children could confess anything without punishment or discussion. His son admitted boyhood mischief. The father admitted burning a table with firecrackers and told how his own father had calmed him about it.

patterns.moment: The player has a chance to speak to {the estranged}, and what is said first decides whether the quarrel ends or sets.
choices: reach out and name what the player did
reach out and say nothing of the quarrel yet
ask {the go-between} to carry a word
patterns.ifNo: Staying silent leaves the quarrel on the tie record with a longer date on it, and {the witness} carries it forward.

patterns.title: The day after the threshold

roles.fill: whoever on the school or work record finishes, fails to finish, or starts: the player, or someone tied to the player. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
whoever on the tie record marks the day: a parent, a child, a partner, a teacher, a principal, a coworker. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
what the records show comes next: a diploma or a second chance at one, a job, college, the army, a training class, or nothing yet

roles.slot: the one who pays or lets it happen
roles.fill: whoever carries the cost or gives the leave: a household member, an employer, a school office

setting.text: Wherever the day is marked, by the records: the stage or the lot where the day ends, the household that evening, the first shift floor. The talk of what comes next happens there or the next morning.

gates: The school or work record shows {the one crossing} finishing, failing to finish, or starting.
{the one who marks it} is tied to {the one crossing} on the records.
{the next step} has a place on the calendar or the opening record.
{the one crossing} has not been asked yet what comes next.
weights: How late in life the threshold came.
Whether the household needs the income now.
Whether a child lives with {the one crossing}.
Whether {the one who pays or lets it happen} has a record of backing the step.

branches.then: The record shows the diploma or the start date and a household or a coworker marks it, unlocking the job or the next training.
The one who marks it asks what happened and what is next, and a second try goes on the calendar if the school or office allows.

branches.when: a principal or teacher offers a way to stay
branches.then: A changed schedule or a retake goes on the school record, and the later job or service reads the diploma.

branches.when: {the one crossing} is the new hire on a shift
branches.then: A coworker or customer's patience on the first day is written, and that person is remembered when the new hire has a say.

branches.when: the player is the one who marks it
branches.then: The player's word, praise or worry, is written on the tie record.

sources.life: A Vietnam-era Marine who worked thirty-five years for a city, he finished high school at seventy-two in night school, keeping a promise to his dying mother. His daughter cheered as he crossed the stage. He then enrolled in college.

A factory worker's daughter who gave birth in her senior year of high school, then went across the country to a top engineering school with her baby. She took the child to day care every morning and studied after bedtime. Her daughter names her as a role model.

She left school in the tenth grade in Vietnam to help her family, immigrated, worked for years, and enrolled in a high school equivalency class at forty-five. Her teacher kept encouraging her after a poor first test. She passed.

A sixteen-year-old in Texas who learned he would be a father, worked two jobs, and planned to drop out for an equivalency test. The principal offered a half-day schedule instead. He graduated with his baby at the ceremony, and the diploma later helped him join the army.

On a first retail job in the Christmas rush she froze at the register. A customer told her to take her time, which let her wait for a coworker to help. She says that patience shaped how she treats people for decades.

patterns.moment: The day ends, and {the one who marks it} asks {the one crossing} what comes next.
choices: name the next step and who helps
say you need a day and a plan
ask {the one who pays or lets it happen} for the room
say it is over and let it rest
patterns.ifNo: Leaving it unnamed writes a drift on the tie record, and the next opening reads it.

patterns.title: The call with an offer

roles.fill: whoever on the work record has a job to fill and calls or meets the player: an employer's office, a hiring manager, a program head, a relative with a business. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
an opening on the place's job record, said with the pay, the hours, and who it serves
whoever depends on the player's income or shares the player's costs, if any: a partner, a parent, a child
whoever the records show spoke for the player: a mentor, a program, a friend inside, or none

setting.text: Wherever the call finds the player, by the records: a phone at home, a missed call returned from the street, a meeting at the offerer's desk, a warehouse floor.

gates: The work record shows the player out of work or looking.
{the offerer} has {the job} open on the job record.
{the offerer} and the player are in touch on the records.
The player has not accepted or refused {the job} yet.
weights: How long the player has been out of work.
How much {the job} pays against the last one.
Whether health cover comes with it.
Whether a household member depends on the income.
Whether {the one who vouched} exists on the records.
Whether the player has a record that employers shun.

branches.then: The job joins the work record from the start date, the household's money record changes, and a first-day scene is placed on the calendar.
The refusal is written and {the offerer} remembers it, and the search record shows more weeks.

branches.when: {the job} pays less than the player's old one
branches.then: The pride and the money are both written, and the household's later votes of confidence read them.

branches.when: {the one who vouched} is on the records
branches.then: A debt of thanks goes on the favor record, and the vouching person is named later.

branches.when: the player is tied to a justice record
branches.then: The offer may exist only because someone chose to take the risk, and that person's trust is written.

sources.life: A twenty-five-year-old near St. Louis who missed a call from a security company's hiring office, returned it, interviewed and was hired as a receptionist at fourteen dollars an hour. The hours let her and her boyfriend share the one car. She still faced a backlog of bills that delayed their plans.

A fifty-year-old with a master's degree who had earned over six figures until his employer collapsed in 2002. After more than a year out and hundreds of applications he took a ten-dollar-an-hour work-from-home job, where take-home would be below his unemployment check. He weighed pride against ending the joblessness.

sources.person: Randy Howland and Jennifer Barfield (a later offer)
sources.life: He was laid off again, then took an offer at about a third of his old pay with benefits, and was dismissed less than a week into training after failing an exam. A woman laid off from IT weighed selling her ring or house, then took a lower-paid job at a law firm.

After nearly five years in prison on drug charges he took whatever work he could find. Housemates in his sober living home invited him to volunteer at a food bank, and in 2021 its director interviewed him and gave him a warehouse job because she believed in him.

patterns.moment: {the offerer} offers {the job}, and the player must say yes or no before the household's bills come due.
choices: accept and ask for the start date
accept and ask for better terms first
say you need a day to talk to the household
patterns.ifNo: A refusal is on the work record, {the offerer} remembers it, and the weeks without work are counted on the household's money record.

patterns.title: The one who is far away

roles.fill: a close tie on the records who lives far off: a parent, sibling, grandparent or old friend. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
whoever on the tie record can carry word between them and the player: a grandparent, a sibling, a cousin
someone who lives with the player and sees the letter, the call or the empty chair

setting.text: Wherever the word lands by the records: a letter on the table, a call on the phone, or the empty chair at a birthday or holiday meal at home.

gates: The tie record shows {the far relative} and the player have not spoken or visited in a long while, or {the far relative} cannot be at a gathering the player's household holds.
The player's household has a gathering on the calendar, or {the far relative} has sent word.
{the go-between} is on the tie record, or the player can write or call directly.
weights: Years since the two last spoke.
Whether the quarrel was about money, a parent's rejection, or a move.
Whether {the far relative} is old, ill, or on duty away (a deployment, a job).
Whether the household has a gathering where the chair stands empty.

branches.when: {the go-between} urges the player to make the first move
branches.then: The player's call or letter is written; the first words are about the future of the tie, not the old dispute, and the tie record warms.

branches.when: the player writes or calls and no answer comes
branches.then: The silence is written on the tie record; the player decides whether to try again or let it rest.
The player decides whether to answer; an answer is read by {household member} and by the tie record.

branches.when: {the far relative} is away on duty and calls by video
branches.then: The call is loud and short; the real talk waits for a quiet moment the player must choose to make.
The reach-out or the refusal is known in town and a rival can read it later.

sources.life: A transgender child and a conservative father spoke only now and then for about 30 years after a divorce. Chick made contact about four years before the recording, they met at a hotel in Salt Lake City and took a two-week road trip through three states. They parted promising to stay in touch.

Childhood friends in Hong Kong wrote weekly letters after Joe's family moved to the U.S. in sixth grade, then lost touch. Decades later Pak, who kept every letter, left messages for 108 people named Joe Chan online; Joe called back. They now meet weekly.

Estranged brothers. Before Derrick deployed to Iraq in 2003 their grandmother urged Raymond to call; both admitted old envy. Derrick later called Raymond from a borrowed satellite phone, and they rebuilt the tie.

The oldest of eight reached out to each sibling as they left or were pushed out of a strict home. The first to call was a younger brother, whom Bryan helped get to college; others resisted for years, and the family slowly became close.

A Maryland National Guard soldier deployed to the southern border left an empty chair at her family's holiday gatherings; the family reached her by video and phone, and her mother held back from calling daily so she would not worry.

A national survey of over 1,300 people and interviews with 100 who repaired rifts: reconciling went best when people looked to the future, set the least they could accept, and set boundaries. Money, in-laws, favoritism and divorce were common causes.

patterns.moment: {the far relative} is far away and the tie is thin: a letter, a call, or an empty chair at the gathering asks the player to make a move.
choices: write or call first and talk about what comes next, not the old dispute
answer {the far relative}'s word but keep a limit on what you will accept
patterns.ifNo: Letting it rest writes a thinner tie. {household member} notices, and the next gathering has the same empty chair.

patterns.title: The new face in the room

roles.fill: a new hire at the player's workplace, a new housemate, or a new neighbor on the records. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
a senior coworker or longtime member of the household or street who knows how things run
the coworkers, housemates or neighbors who are there when the newcomer arrives

setting.text: Wherever the newcomer lands by the records: a workplace floor or break room, the doorway of the house, or a front gate and yard.

gates: {the newcomer} is new to the player's workplace, household or street on the records.
The player works, lives or has a home there.
{the old hand} or {the group} is on the record.
weights: How much of the place's work or housework the newcomer will share with the player.
Whether the player has been the newcomer in the past.
Whether others on the record are also new.
Hours the two will spend together in a week.

branches.when: {the group} includes the newcomer in meals or outings in the first weeks
branches.then: The newcomer's ties on the record grow and later help the player.

branches.when: the player is the one who shows them how things run
branches.then: The newcomer remembers who taught them and owes the player a small favor.

branches.when: nobody makes room for the newcomer
branches.then: The newcomer's support falls in the first weeks, and a leaving record may follow.

branches.when: the newcomer is a stranger who knocks first with a gift or a question
branches.then: A neighbor tie forms on the record, with shared interests and talk about the street.

branches.when: the newcomer is from a different background
branches.then: The talk goes personal, and a hard story shared leaves both with a closer tie.

sources.life: A University of Illinois study of engineers at a large manufacturer: about 65 percent of what new hires learned came from coworkers and 15 percent from managers. A local mentor, a meaningful early assignment and social invitations outside work helped; many newcomers left in two years.
A woman of 55 renovating a new house in Detroit heard a knock; her neighbor in her 90s brought a gift and the two found a shared love of architecture and became best friends.

Next-door neighbors for years without meeting. Their dogs met at the gate; a 79-year-old asked a 31-year-old for advice on talking with her grandson, and both told hard stories. The older woman said the friendship changed her plans for her future.

A University of Kansas study of 467 people (355 adults who had recently moved): moving from acquaintance to casual friend took roughly 40 to 60 hours together, and work hours counted for much less than relaxed time.

patterns.moment: {the newcomer} comes over to introduce themselves and the player decides how much room to make.
choices: show them how things run and introduce them to {the group}
invite them to something outside the work or house
leave them to find their own way
patterns.ifNo: Leaving them to find their own way writes a thin tie; they learn from whoever else is there, and the player is the one who did not make room.

patterns.title: Asked along

roles.fill: a friend or new acquaintance on the records who asks the player to come along. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
someone the player is seeing for a first date, a new partner on the tie record, said with that tie
a parent or relative who is already at the place the player is asked to, if the records show one

setting.text: Wherever the asking leads by the records: a meal, an outing, a ride, a favor at someone's house, or a public place or venue for a first date.

gates: {the one who asks} or {the one who is met} is on the tie record.
The player has free hours in the week.
The place is one the world has (a restaurant, a house, a park, a venue).
weights: Hours the two have already spent together in relaxed time.
Whether the player is alone on the day (a holiday).

branches.when: the player says yes and goes
branches.then: The tie moves up a rung on the tie record; more hours follow.

branches.when: the player goes and {their family} is there
branches.then: The family reads the player's manners, and its view is written on the tie record.
The tie stays where it is and the ask is not repeated soon.

branches.when: the ask is a favor, not a visit
branches.then: How the player answers is the test of the tie and is remembered.

branches.when: the one who asks needs help and has been helped before
branches.then: The player's patience is written; a deep tie forms.

branches.when: the first date goes well and one asks the other to a family meal
branches.then: The invitation is written on the tie; the answer sets whether the other is brought into the household's circle.

sources.life: Hall's study: relaxed time together builds friendship far more than time working together. He says you cannot make people spend time with you, but you can invite them, and suggests changing the setting, such as lunch, to show you want the friendship.

Two men who met online, 19 years apart in age, set a first date for Christmas Eve 2010. Afterward Seth said his mother was hosting dinner, because nobody should be alone on Christmas. Octavius felt at home with the family and proposed three Christmases later.

A man holding a sign at a highway ramp was given money and food, then invited home on New Year's Eve. Four years later his friend talked him into moving in, and they were close until the end of his life.
The neighbor's first move was a knock at the door and a gift; the friendship grew from there.

Two men met online and had a first date on Christmas Eve despite a gap in age. He called it amazing, and afterward the other invited him to Christmas dinner with his mother, saying no one should be alone on Christmas.

patterns.moment: {the one who asks} asks the player along, and the answer is the first test of the tie.
choices: say yes and bring a small thing for {their family}
patterns.ifNo: Saying no plainly writes the tie as it was; the ask may not come again soon.

patterns.title: News of a baby

roles.fill: a close tie on the records who is expecting or has just had a baby, who may be the player. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.

roles.slot: the one who is told first
roles.fill: whoever the records show hears first: a mother, a partner, an aunt
the aunts, uncles and grandparents on the tie record who hear after

setting.text: Wherever the telling or the birth lands by the records: a kitchen table, a phone call, or a hospital waiting room.

gates: {the parent-to-be} is on the tie record and a baby is on the way or born.
{the one who is told first} is on the records.
The relatives are not all in one place.
weights: Age and money of the parent-to-be.
Whether the birth came early or with risk.
Whether the baby is welcome to {the relatives}.
Whether anyone near is ill or has died.

branches.when: {the one who is told first} keeps the secret
branches.then: The telling happens on {the parent-to-be}'s own time and the tie holds.

branches.when: {the one who is told first} tells the rest
branches.then: A rift opens between them and {the parent-to-be}'s side; hurt relatives later come round and help.

branches.when: the birth is early or at risk
branches.then: Visitors are limited; the family's help comes as prayer, a call chain or food, and the household's cost record rises.

branches.when: a relative asks the player for help or a promise
branches.then: The answer is written on the favor record and the player's word is remembered.
The news and what the player does for the family is on the town's record.

branches.when: relatives, neighbors or friends offer to share the care of the baby
branches.then: The new parent has more rest and less isolation on the household record, and the helpers earn a favor owed; if nobody offers, the isolation is written.

sources.life: A college junior of 19 told her mother first and asked her to tell the family. One aunt kept the secret then told others, causing a rift with her mother; other aunts were hurt but threw a baby shower. The family's blessing came before the birth.

A baby born at about 28 weeks in the Davenport, Iowa, area. Staff limited visitors, so only Kelly's mother was at the birth. A prayer chain started by a grandmother helped, the baby avoided intensive care, and he went home after two days.

sources.person: Mbendjele families, as reported by researchers
sources.life: A study of hunter-gatherers in Congo found babies had about eight regular hands-on caregivers besides their mothers, with help arriving within seconds of a cry. Researchers argue that parents without that circle, mostly in Western homes, face more isolation and postpartum depression.

patterns.moment: News of a baby reaches the family and {the parent-to-be} asks the player for help, a visit or a promise.
choices: promise a visit and a hand
ask what is needed and give it
patterns.ifNo: Staying out writes a gap on the tie record; {the relatives} notice who came.

patterns.title: The last day

roles.fill: whoever on the records is leaving a job, a school or the town: the player or a close tie. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
coworkers, classmates, neighbors or a best friend who stay
whoever in charge on the records decides how the day is marked, said with the role

setting.text: Wherever the leaving happens by the records: a break room, a classroom doorway, a front yard with boxes, a clinic or office for the last name on a list.

gates: {the one who leaves} is on the work, school or home record and the leaving date is set.
{the ones left behind} are on the tie record.
The leaving is chosen or required by orders, a closing or a move.
weights: Whether {the one who leaves} is a child.
Whether a send-off is the place's custom.

branches.when: the leaving is a child's move with orders
branches.then: A list of people to say goodbye to is made and each is met on a chosen day; a small kindness from one lifts the whole move.
A mess of tears on the last day; the leaver wants to be left alone for a while, and the tie lasts through letters.

branches.when: the leaving is a retirement or a quit
branches.then: The send-off is mixed: pride and sadness together; regrets about missed years show up.

branches.when: the old tie is lost and found again years later
branches.then: Letters kept long afterward bring a reunion and the tie resumes where it left off.
The last day of an office or a staff job is read in the town's record.

sources.life: In sixth grade Joe's family left Hong Kong for the U.S. The friends wrote weekly at first and then lost touch; decades later Pak, who kept every letter, found Joe, and they now bike and eat together weekly.

A five-year-old Army child moving from Virginia to Alabama made a list of people to hug and have sign it, ending with his pediatrician, who called and met him on her supper break. The mother said the small gesture eased the move.

sources.person: A military spouse and her 12-year-old daughter
sources.life: On the last day of school the daughter's best friend was moving away; she wished the family would move too, and asked to be left alone to cry. Her mother stayed available.
A New York Times Magazine piece on retirement: send-offs vary and the old gold-watch custom has mostly gone; some had parties, others regretted missed time with their children, and it is often sad.

A public relations worker left a nonprofit after nearly twenty years when leaders reversed promises about working from home. He would miss his supervisor of more than ten years and his work friends, and took a new job in six weeks.

patterns.moment: It is the last day, and {the ones left behind} ask {the one who leaves} what comes next.
choices: say goodbye to each by name
leave a way to keep in touch
ask {the ones left behind} for a promise to write
patterns.ifNo: Leaving quietly writes that no one was told; the tie fades, and the first letter after will have to be the player's.

patterns.title: Trust broken in front of people

roles.fill: a friend, coworker or relative on the tie record who broke a promise or named the player as the one at fault. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
a friend or lawyer on the record who stays with the player
the people at the school, work or street who see it happen
a paper or a camera on the record, if the matter is public

setting.text: Wherever the break lands by the records: at school or work with onlookers, in the street, or at home. A public accusation reaches the home door by paper and camera.

gates: {the one who broke it} is on the tie record, or the player is named as at fault by someone who knows them.
A promise on the record was broken, or a charge was made.
{the onlookers} are on the record.
weights: Whether the charge is true on the record.

branches.when: the player confronts the one who broke it
branches.then: A confrontation is the most common answer; the player's anger is written and may cut the tie.

branches.when: the one who broke it makes amends
branches.then: Forgiveness is easier when anger is lower, the apology sincere and the cause clear; the tie is written as mended.

branches.when: the charge is false and public
branches.then: {the press} and {the onlookers} carry the charge; the player's name is hurt even after it is cleared, and {the one who stands by} is remembered for life.
The silence is read as agreement by onlookers; a witness later tells the story.
The break is a past a rival may use.

branches.when: the accusation is made in writing or in private, before anyone asks the player's side
branches.then: The player decides whether to answer in writing, ask a third person how the conclusion was reached, or let it stand; the unanswered paper is read later.

sources.life: A quantitative study of over 900 accounts of betrayal from British, French and Swiss participants: partners (about 30 percent) and close friends (about 27 percent) were the most common betrayers; confronting and cutting ties were the commonest reactions, and forgiveness seemed possible when anger was lower.

A security guard first praised for clearing people from a bomb at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics was named the FBI's suspect. Papers ran headlines and crews camped at his door, where he lived with his mother. His friend and attorney stood by him; he was cleared but said it could not restore his name.

sources.person: A worker writing to a business columnist
sources.life: A worker was accused without being asked for their side, lost a bonus and was told to sign a final write-up; supervisors then acted as if nothing happened. The columnist advised signing for receipt only, sending a calm written reply and asking a supervisor not involved how the conclusion was reached.

patterns.moment: {the one who broke it} has broken trust or named the player as at fault, and the player answers in front of {the onlookers}.
choices: confront them now and say what it cost
hear them out and ask what they will do
keep your word and say nothing yet
bring {the one who stands by} and answer the charge in the open
patterns.ifNo: Silence writes the tie as cooling. {the onlookers} carry the story without the player's side.

patterns.title: The morning after the late meeting

roles.fill: a partner or parent at home on the household record, said with what they are to the player. Introduced the first time with full name and what they are to the player.
the place's own council, board or legislature, by its own name
any child in the house, if the record shows one

setting.text: The kitchen or doorway at home the morning after the night meeting, or the phone when the player is away.

gates: The player holds an office on {the body} that meets at night or away from home.
{household member} is on the household record.
The calendar shows a night meeting or a trip that ran late or kept the player away.
weights: Whether {household member} has a job and its hours.
Whether the pay of the office is low and the player has another job.

branches.when: {household member} has been doing the dinners and the pickups
branches.then: They say plainly what the nights cost; the player's answer is written, and a plan for time or a shared schedule may follow.

branches.when: the player keeps a night free for the family
branches.then: The household record warms and the change is told to {the body}.

branches.when: {the children} miss the player at school events
branches.then: The children's tie falls until the player makes it up.
A rival may read out the absences later; {household member} may not support the next race.
{household member} says it is worth it; the support is written as a favor owed.
